title: The Woman Whose Heart Failed After Months of Heavy Bleeding — Iron Deficiency Anemia and a Failing Heart

sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content:
She is 47 years old, presenting with abdominal distension for three days that has progressed to whole-body swelling, along with breathlessness for two days. She had been apparently well four years earlier, when she had an episode of fever with generalized swelling requiring hospitalization; blood transfusion was advised at that time but she declined, opting instead for iron injections. Earlier this year, she saw a gynecologist for abnormal uterine bleeding (heavy periods, using four pads a day) and had an ultrasound done. She had a viral prodrome roughly three weeks before this presentation.

She had been taking an anti-inflammatory medication for two days, after which she developed fever, loss of appetite, and muscle aches. This was followed by abdominal distension, then swelling in her legs and face, and breathlessness for the last two days, along with palpitations for two days. She denies chest pain, frothy urine, waking at night to urinate, painful urination, fainting, or cold hands and feet.

She has no known diabetes, asthma, or tuberculosis, and no history of blood transfusion. She had a tubectomy 23 years ago. She has decreased appetite, eats a mixed diet, and has regular bowel and bladder habits, with no addictions or known allergies. She reached menarche at 13, married at 14, and had her first child at 18, going on to have four pregnancies. Her most recent period was heavy, with a 5-day cycle on a 28-day pattern, using four pads a day.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
- **General exam:** conscious and well-oriented; pallor present; bilateral pedal edema above the ankles; platynychia (flattened nails); no icterus, clubbing, cyanosis, or lymphadenopathy; height 149 cm, weight 45 kg, BMI 20.3
- **Vitals:** temperature 98.4°F, pulse 96 bpm regular, blood pressure 170/80 mmHg in the right arm, respiratory rate 24/min; tongue appeared pale with a bluish tinge
- **Cardiovascular exam:** apex beat at the 5th intercostal space with a palpable thrill; loud S1 and P2; an S3 that accentuated with inspiration on the right side and with expiration on the left; a cervical venous hum present
- **Respiratory exam:** normal vesicular breath sounds with bilateral fine crackles in the axillary, infra-axillary, and infrascapular areas
- **Abdominal exam:** distended, with a palpable liver and spleen; normal bowel sounds
- **Renal function and electrolytes:** urea 20 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, uric acid 4.0 mg/dL, calcium 9.6 mg/dL, phosphorus 2.7 mg/dL, sodium 144 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 106 mEq/L
- **Blood counts:** hemoglobin severely low at 4.4 g/dL, total leukocyte count 5,600 cells/cumm, platelets 1.6 lakh/cumm, RBC 2.97 million/cumm, PCV 16.6%, MCV 55.9 fl, MCH 14.9 pg; smear showed anisopoikilocytosis with microcytic hypochromic cells, pencil forms, and teardrop cells, consistent with microcytic hypochromic anemia
- **Liver function:** total bilirubin 0.42 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.16 mg/dL, AST 17 IU/L, ALT 15 IU/L, ALP 163 IU/L, total protein 6.3 g/dL, albumin 3.6 g/dL
- **Blood group:** A positive
- **2D echocardiogram:** concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (wall thickness 1.4 cm), moderate to severe tricuspid regurgitation with an estimated right ventricular systolic pressure of 65 mmHg, moderate pulmonary artery hypertension, mild aortic and mitral regurgitation, preserved ejection fraction at 63%, and a minimal pericardial effusion

**Working diagnosis at admission:** acute left heart failure causing right heart failure with systemic arterial hypertension.

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded on the Ward
sections.content:
She was started on IV furosemide and a calcium channel blocker (nifedipine), with vitals monitored every four hours and strict fluid intake/output charting. On transfer to the ward the following day, her dyspnea and swelling had significantly improved. Her working diagnosis was refined to acute left heart failure likely secondary to acute iron deficiency anemia from excessive menstrual blood loss, with viral myocarditis also considered. Because she continued to decline blood transfusion, she was managed with oral iron replacement (ferrous fumarate), with her total iron deficit calculated using the Ganzoni formula.

Over the following days her dry cough, decreased sleep, and generalized weakness persisted while her breathlessness gradually eased, and she continued on furosemide, an expectorant syrup, and oral iron replacement with regular vital sign monitoring.
